subject: Medicine
summary: Coeliac disease is an immune‑mediated enteropathy triggered by gluten in genetically predisposed people, causing villous atrophy and malabsorption. Diagnosis relies on serology and duodenal biopsy, and lifelong gluten avoidance is curative.

sections.p: Coeliac disease is an autoimmune disorder where ingestion of gluten (wheat, barley, rye) leads to small‑bowel mucosal injury. Diagnosis requires compatible symptoms, positive serology, and confirmatory duodenal biopsy.
b: Serology: IgA anti‑tTG and IgA anti‑endomysial antibodies; total IgA to rule out deficiency.
Biopsy: Marsh 3 lesions (villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, intraepithelial lymphocytosis).

t.b: Does the patient have antibodies against tissue transglutaminase? Positive (>10 U) supports diagnosis; negative with IgA deficiency needs IgG‑based testing.
What is the histology of the proximal small bowel? Marsh 3 confirms disease; normal mucosa argues against it.
Is the patient genetically predisposed? Absence essentially excludes coeliac disease.

sections.p: Severity is graded by histology (Marsh classification) and clinical impact (symptom burden, nutrient deficiencies). Staging guides urgency of treatment and monitoring.
b: Marsh 0‑1: potential or early disease; may need repeat testing.
Marsh 2‑3: established disease; start gluten‑free diet immediately.

sections.p: The primary trigger is dietary gluten in a genetically susceptible host. No other single cause, but co‑existing conditions can mimic or exacerbate malabsorption.
b: HLA‑DQ2/DQ8 positivity (≈95 % of patients).
Environmental trigger: gluten ingestion.
Associated disorders: type 1 diabetes, autoimmune thyroid disease, IBD, Behçet disease.

sections.p: Presentation varies with age and nutritional status. Classic features are chronic diarrhoea, weight loss, and abdominal bloating; extra‑intestinal signs include anemia, osteoporosis, dermatitis herpetiformis, and infertility.
b: Gastrointestinal: watery diarrhoea, steatorrhoea, abdominal pain.
Hematologic: iron‑deficiency anemia, folate/B12 deficiency.
Dermatologic: itchy papulovesicular rash on elbows/knees.

sections.p: A stepwise approach starts with serology, proceeds to endoscopy with biopsy, and adds supportive labs to assess complications.
b: Baseline CBC, ferritin, vitamin D, calcium, folate, B12.
Bone density scan if risk factors for osteoporosis.

t.b: Is iron deficiency present? Low ferritin confirms iron‑deficiency anemia, a common complication.
Is there vitamin D deficiency? Low levels indicate malabsorption and risk of bone disease.
What is bone mineral density? Low T‑score signals osteopenia/osteoporosis needing calcium/vit D supplementation.

sections.p: If untreated, coeliac disease can lead to severe malnutrition, refractory disease, and malignancy. Recognise warning signs that demand urgent evaluation.
b: Unexplained weight loss >10 % in 3 months.
Severe anemia or electrolyte disturbances.
New‑onset neurological signs (ataxia, seizures).

sections.p: The cornerstone is a strict, lifelong gluten‑free diet (GFD). Adjuncts address deficiencies and refractory disease.
b: Gluten‑free diet: eliminates wheat, barley, rye; restores mucosa.
Nutrient repletion: oral iron, folic acid, vitamin D, calcium as needed.
Refractory disease: consider short‑course steroids; avoid unnecessary immunosuppressants.

sections.p: Regular review ensures dietary adherence, monitors recovery, and screens for complications.
b: Serology (IgA tTG) at 6‑12 months to confirm response.
Repeat biopsy only if symptoms persist despite strict GFD.
Screen for osteoporosis every 2‑3 years in adults.

sections.p: Several conditions mimic coeliac disease’s gastrointestinal and nutritional picture.
b: Irritable bowel syndrome – functional pain without malabsorption.
Inflammatory bowel disease – ulceration, not villous atrophy.
Lactose intolerance – diarrhoea after dairy, not gluten.

sections.p: Certain laboratory or histologic findings may be falsely reassuring.
b: IgA deficiency can give false‑negative IgA tTG; use IgG‑based tests.
Partial villous atrophy (Marsh 1‑2) may be missed on limited biopsies.
Serology can normalize before full mucosal healing; do not stop diet early.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden collapse with anemia or electrolyte imbalance

faq.q: Can adults develop coeliac disease if they have eaten gluten all life?
faq.a: Yes; it can present at any age after a trigger such as infection, pregnancy, or increased gluten exposure.

faq.q: Is a gluten‑free diet enough for all patients?
faq.a: For most, yes; refractory cases need specialist input and possibly short‑term steroids.

faq.q: Do I need to avoid oats?
faq.a: Pure, uncontaminated oats are usually safe, but many commercial oats are cross‑contaminated with wheat.

exam: Describe the pathophysiological cascade from gluten ingestion to villous atrophy in coeliac disease.
List the diagnostic criteria for coeliac disease, including serology and histology.
Explain the management steps for a newly diagnosed patient, emphasizing dietary counseling and monitoring for complications.
